issues.description: The abstract and multiple sections describe the sample as a 'national probability sample' and 'nationally representative sample,' but the Methods section states participants were 'recruited through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington' with an average age of 19 years and 68% female. This is clearly a student convenience sample, not a national probability sample. This is a fundamental contradiction that undermines the entire framing of the paper, including claims about generalizability to the general population.
issues.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington... the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female.

issues.subcategory: False generalizability claims from student sample
issues.description: The paper repeatedly claims the results are from a 'general population sample' and are 'highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.' However, the sample is a university student sample (mean age 19, recruited from introductory psychology). This directly contradicts the paper's own theoretical argument that SDO-environmentalism associations are stronger in general population samples than student samples, and undermines the stated rationale for the study (to extend findings beyond student samples).
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.description: The entire rationale for the study is to extend Stanley et al.'s [14] student-sample findings to a general population sample, and the paper frames its contribution as using 'a large, national probability sample.' Yet the actual sample is a student sample very similar to Stanley et al.'s. The paper then interprets results as consistent with expectations for general population samples, when the sample is actually a student sample. This invalidates the core contribution claimed.
issues.quote: We expand on Stanley et al.'s study by using a large, national probability sample spanning five years to examine how these variables relate over time in the general population.

issues.subcategory: Mismatch between described measure and actual items
issues.description: The abstract and much of the paper describe the outcome as 'willingness to change behaviour to benefit the environment' or 'willingness to sacrifice for the environment,' but the actual items measure environmental concern ('How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?') and perceived exaggeration of environmental problems. These are attitudinal/perceptual items, not measures of behavioral willingness or sacrifice. The construct label does not match the operationalization.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] environmental concern scale, 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'

issues.description: The environmentalism measure consists of only two items, one of which is reverse-scored. No reliability estimate is reported for this two-item scale, and two items provide very limited measurement of the construct. While reliabilities for SDO and RWA are mentioned (and appear in Table 1), the reliability of .76 shown for WILL in Table 1 seems surprisingly high for a two-item scale measuring somewhat different aspects (concern vs. perceived exaggeration), and no discussion of this is provided.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems.

issues.description: The chi-square difference test comparing the cross-lagged effects of SDO on RWA versus RWA on SDO yields χ²(1) = 15,389.13, which is extraordinarily large and implausible for a single degree of freedom test in a sample of 374 participants. This value appears to be an error, possibly a typo or computational mistake. A chi-square difference this large would be virtually impossible with this sample size.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)

issues.description: The Data Analysis section states 'we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings,' but Figure 1's caption states 'All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.' These are contradictory significance thresholds.
issues.quote: we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings... All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.

issues.description: The chi-square difference test comparing SDO vs. RWA as predictors of environmentalism was non-significant (χ²(1) = 2.34, p = .126), yet the authors interpret SDO as a 'stronger predictor' and throughout the discussion treat this as a confirmed finding. A non-significant difference test means the null hypothesis of equal predictive strength cannot be rejected, directly contradicting the interpretation.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.

issues.description: The CFI of .86 is below the conventional threshold of .90 (and well below the more stringent .95 threshold). While the authors acknowledge this and point to RMSEA and SRMR as indicating good fit, a CFI this low suggests meaningful misfit. The justification that indices 'less influenced by complexity' show good fit is not sufficient, as CFI is a standard fit index and its poor value raises concerns about model specification.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07)

issues.subcategory: Use of listwise deletion with longitudinal data
issues.description: The authors report using listwise deletion for a five-wave longitudinal study. Longitudinal studies typically suffer from substantial attrition, and listwise deletion can introduce severe bias if data are not missing completely at random (MCAR). Full information maximum likelihood (FIML) or multiple imputation would be more appropriate and would preserve statistical power. No justification for this choice or analysis of missing data patterns is provided.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.description: For a five-year longitudinal study, no information is provided about attrition rates, how many participants were present at each wave, or whether those who dropped out differed systematically from those who remained. The only mention is that 'Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website,' which is insufficient for evaluating the study's validity.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.subcategory: Sample size inconsistency with confidence interval precision
issues.description: The reported sample size is N = 374, yet the confidence intervals in Table 1 are extremely narrow (e.g., SD of SDO = .96 [.95, .98]), suggesting a much larger sample. With N = 374, confidence intervals for correlations and descriptive statistics would typically be wider. This raises questions about whether the reported N is correct or whether the confidence intervals were computed incorrectly.
issues.quote: Of the 374 participants included in this study... SD .96 [.95, .98]

issues.subcategory: Missing RWA item at one time point not addressed
issues.description: One RWA item was not assessed at Time 2, meaning the RWA measure differs across time points. This is problematic for longitudinal comparisons and the stationarity constraints imposed on the model. No discussion of how this was handled analytically or its potential impact on results is provided.
issues.quote: The item 'Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the "normal way" things are supposed to be done', was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.subcategory: Path analysis instead of latent variable model
issues.description: The authors use path analysis (observed variables) rather than structural equation modeling with latent variables. With abbreviated scales (6 items for SDO, 6 for RWA, 2 for environmentalism), measurement error is substantial. Using observed composites in cross-lagged models can bias cross-lagged estimates, typically attenuating them. A latent variable approach would better account for measurement error.
issues.quote: We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment.

issues.subcategory: Causal claims from cross-lagged panel model
issues.description: The authors make causal claims based on cross-lagged panel models, stating 'These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism.' Cross-lagged panel models do not establish causation, and recent methodological literature (e.g., Hamaker et al., 2015) has shown that traditional CLPM conflates between-person and within-person effects, making causal interpretation problematic. The authors do not acknowledge these limitations.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism. The motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance

issues.description: The traditional cross-lagged panel model used here does not separate within-person change from stable between-person differences. The random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM; Hamaker et al., 2015) addresses this limitation and is now considered more appropriate for making inferences about within-person processes. The failure to use or at least consider this approach is a notable limitation.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.description: The authors state 'We present standardized parameters' but then report unstandardized parameters (B values) in the results. Figure 1 is described as showing 'Unstandardized parameters.' This inconsistency makes it unclear which parameters are being reported where.
issues.quote: We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances... Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment

issues.subcategory: Reporting SD instead of SE for parameter estimates
issues.description: The authors report 'SD' alongside parameter estimates (e.g., 'B = -.11, SD = .01'), but standard practice is to report standard errors (SE) for regression coefficients, not standard deviations. This appears to be either a labeling error or a misunderstanding of the output.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01])

issues.subcategory: Confidence interval inconsistency for RWA path
issues.description: The reported confidence interval for the RWA to environmentalism path is [-.05, -.01], but the point estimate is B = -.02. While the point estimate falls within this CI, the interval is asymmetric around the estimate in a way that seems unusual for a normally distributed parameter estimate with SE = .01 (which would yield approximately [-.04, .00]).

The Data Analysis section contains a duplicated sentence about constraining cross-lagged associations, suggesting a copy-editing error that may indicate incomplete revision of the methods description.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point... Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.

issues.description: The paper references the NZAVS (New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study) website for sample details and states the Mplus syntax will be available on the NZAVS website. The NZAVS is a well-known national probability study, but the described sample is a student convenience sample. This suggests either the wrong sample description was included, or the paper conflates two different datasets.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.description: The reported RMSEA is .03, but the 90% confidence interval is [.025, .026], which is impossibly narrow and does not contain the point estimate of .03. This appears to be a reporting error.

The discussion interprets findings as showing SDO is a stronger predictor than RWA in the 'general population,' consistent with Stanley and Wilson's [22] meta-analytic finding. However, if the sample is actually students (as described in Methods), this interpretation is backwards—the meta-analysis showed RWA should be the stronger predictor in student samples, which would make the current findings inconsistent with, not supportive of, the meta-analytic results.
issues.quote: This pattern of results, where SDO is a stronger predictor than RWA, is the reverse of the pattern obtained from the first longitudinal analysis on this topic, which showed that RWA was the stronger predictor among students [14]. However, this difference in findings is consistent with expectations based on the results of Stanley and Wilson's [22] meta-analysis

issues.description: No pre-registration is mentioned for this study. Given the multiple possible model specifications, significance thresholds, and analytic choices (e.g., which constraints to impose, whether to use listwise deletion vs. FIML), the absence of pre-registration raises concerns about undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom.

The autoregressive (stability) paths are described as showing variables are 'relatively stable over time' but no specific parameter estimates are reported in the text for these paths. Only the cross-lagged paths are numerically reported.
issues.quote: SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time, consistent with our prediction that these variables remain largely unchanged over the study period.

issues.subcategory: Missing correlation table for all time points
issues.description: Only Time 1 descriptive statistics and correlations are presented. For a five-wave longitudinal study, correlations across all time points would be important for evaluating the data and understanding patterns of association over time.
issues.quote: Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1.

issues.description: Environmentalism is measured with only two items, one measuring concern and one measuring perceived exaggeration. This is a very thin operationalization of a complex construct, and the two items may tap different facets (genuine concern vs. skepticism). This limits construct validity and reliability of the environmentalism measure.
issues.quote: 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'

issues.description: The model chi-square is 36,511.73 with 2,279 degrees of freedom for a sample of N = 374. This chi-square to sample size ratio is extremely large and unusual. With N = 374, a chi-square this large would indicate severe model misfit or suggest the sample size is actually much larger than reported.

The authors state they adopted p < .05 'Because of the large sample size of this dataset,' but p < .05 is the standard threshold and a large sample would typically warrant a more stringent threshold, not the standard one. The justification is backwards.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.
